Talk/Poster Title: Single-molecule CTCF occupancy and zinc-finger engagement are separable dimensions of chromatin boundary activity
Abstract: CTCF and cohesin are major organizers of three-dimensional genome architecture. Cohesin extrudes chromatin loops, and DNA-bound CTCF acts as a directional boundary that can pause or retain cohesin. Yet CTCF sites are neither constitutively occupied nor perfectly impermeable to cohesin, making both CTCF binding and boundary activity probabilistic. The molecular determinants underlying these two layers of heterogeneity remain incompletely understood. Here, we analyze Fiber-seq, a single-molecule chromatin footprinting approach, to quantify CTCF occupancy and zinc-finger (ZF)-DNA engagement on individual native DNA molecules. We find that CTCF occupancy is jointly shaped by sequence affinity, CpG methylation, and local chromatin context, with allele-specific binding providing an internal validation of these determinants. Beyond occupancy, single-molecule protection patterns reveal recurrent CTCF ZF-DNA engagement states whose relative abundance varies across genomic loci and is influenced by local sequence context. Importantly, N-terminal ZF engagement provides additional information about RAD21 enrichment, insulation strength, and chromatin loop strength beyond CTCF occupancy. Together, these results establish two quantitative dimensions of endogenous CTCF binding: occupancy determines how frequently a CTCF barrier is present, whereas the DNA-engagement state of bound CTCF provides a second layer associated with its functional effectiveness as a cohesin boundary.

Talk/Poster Title: DeepPBS-AF3: Bridging structure- and sequence-based models of protein-DNA binding specificity with AlphaFold 3
Abstract: Predicting DNA-binding specificity of a transcription factor (TF) is a challenging yet essential task for understanding gene regulation. While sequence-based models utilize abundant high-throughput binding data, the diversity of protein folds and binding-associated conformational changes motivate approaches that use 3D structural information. Previous work, DeepPBS, addresses this by predicting binding specificity as a position weight matrix (PWM) directly from protein-DNA complexes, by encoding their physicochemical and geometric interactions. Its training, however, is heavily limited by the scarcity of experimental TF-DNA co-crystal structures. Here, we introduce DeepPBS-AF3, which leverages AlphaFold 3 (AF3) to generate structural inputs for TFs that lack experimental complexes. This approach enables DeepPBS-AF3 to be trained on AF3-predicted complexes and extends its applicability to binding specificity prediction with sequence inputs. When trained on AF3-predicted structures, DeepPBS-AF3 demonstrates greater accuracy and generalizability over DeepPBS. Furthermore, we present a workflow that predicts binding specificity for a TF without a known binding DNA sequence. Together, our results establish structure prediction as a viable approach to overcome the scarcity of experimental structures in structure-based prediction of binding specificity, with potential extension to other applications such as predicting binding affinity and binding sites.

Talk/Poster Title: VHSeek: Biology foundation model-based virus representations revealing virus host associations
Abstract: Virus-host association prediction is fundamental to virus-related disease control and phage therapy, yet many existing tools require candidate-host genome sequences, which may be unavailable for some eukaryotic hosts or impractical to search at the scale of large virome studies. We present VHSeek, a supervised virus-host association predictor that integrates DNA- and protein-derived viral representations. VHSeek combines nucleotide representations from AIDO.DNA and protein representations from ESM2 to learn virus-host association patterns, and then transfers predictions through known host taxonomies from lower to higher ranks. During inference, VHSeek uses viral sequence data and known host taxonomies, without host sequence data. Compared with iPHoP, the state-of-the-art baseline evaluated in this study, VHSeek improves genus-level maximum F1 score (Fmax), Top-1 accuracy, and area under the precision--recall curve (AUPR) by 12%, 19%, and 27%, respectively. Confidence thresholding enables abstention and reduces false discoveries. On the processed IMG/VR v4.1 metagenomic collection, VHSeek expands effective host coverage from 36.5% to 64.5% using a validation-calibrated confidence threshold. VHSeek prioritizes candidate viruses and reservoir hosts with potential human health impacts, including multi-host hypotheses in which one virus may be associated with humans and additional hosts (e.g., Saboya virus with Homo sapiens and Culicidae) not currently captured in the dataset.

Cell cycle phase is an understudied source of variation in gene expression. EMT is a case in point: this cell state transition that drives metastasis has been studied widely across tissue, stimulus, and microenvironmental conditions, yet cell cycle effects are routinely regressed out of single-cell EMT analyses. Here, we compare EMT between G1 and cycling (S/G2/M) cell states in two independent scRNA-seq datasets of TGF-?-stimulated MCF10A mammary epithelial cells (varying dose and timepoint). G1 cells consistently show higher expression of EMT genes and upregulated RNA velocities than cycling cells, with the strongest upregulation in G1 EMT intermediate states. Consistent with the go-or-grow hypothesis, EMT and cell cycle programs inversely correlate; moreover, this anticorrelation extends to RNA velocity and strengthens with TGF-? dose. We identify a 77-gene G1-specific EMT signature enriched for actin cytoskeletal and extracellular matrix genes that would otherwise be lost by regressing out cell cycle effects. This gene set prompts the hypothesis that, unconstrained by the cytoskeletal demands of mitosis, G1 cells have greater capacity to execute EMT. Further, we developed an EMT gene regulatory model coupled with a cell cycle module, and found through simulation that the model recapitulated this inverse EMT-cell cycle relationship. Using this model, we predict that cycle-selective chemotherapy enriches for the G1 intermediate state, which has high metastatic potential. Cell cycle phase thus ought not be regressed out of EMT states, given its influence on EMT.

Talk/Poster Title: NMD-targeted isoforms define a post-transcriptional dosage-control layer for highly coordinated human genes
Abstract: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) contributes to gene expression regulation, but how the potential for NMD regulation relates to network connectivity and sensitivity to gene disruption remains unclear. Here, we integrated human transcript annotations, GTEx co-expression networks, Cancer Dependency Map measurements, and functional and proteomic resources to examine whether genes with annotated NMD-targeted isoforms show distinct connectivity–dependency relationships. After accounting for transcript number, expression level and variability, and common-essential status, we found that highly connected NMD-positive genes showed greater cellular dependency than their less connected counterparts. This connectivity association was stronger in NMD-positive genes than in genes without annotated NMD isoforms and was broadly observed across tissue contexts. Functional analyses linked high-degree NMD-positive genes to protein complexes and RNA-processing pathways. Within NMD-positive genes, highly connected genes also showed lower RNA-adjusted protein abundance in both normal-tissue and cancer proteomic datasets. Together, our findings associate annotated NMD potential with network connectivity, cellular dependency, and protein output, providing a framework for investigating how RNA regulation relates to sensitivity to gene disruption.

Talk/Poster Title: Making Every Dock Count: Two Strategies for Enriching Gigascale Synthon-Based Virtual Screening
Abstract:
Make-on-demand chemical spaces have grown past 10^10 compounds, and V-SYNTHES makes them tractable by docking the Minimal Enumeration Library (MEL) first and expanding only the top-scoring scaffolds into full ligands. In practice, however, a one-million-compound docking budget is exhausted by the ligands enumerated from very few top-scoring MEL scaffolds, leaving the vast majority of comparably promising scaffolds untouched.

We address this bottleneck from two directions.

The first reallocates the budget by proxy score. Prescreening tools rank enumerated ligands cheaply, but general-purpose deep-learning prescreeners are trained once across a broad population of complexes and applied unmodified to every pocket, so their benefit depends on how closely a target resembles that population. We propose a target-specific alternative: MEL-Steered PharmacoNet fine-tunes PharmacoNet to a single pocket using the fragment-docking evidence the pipeline already produces and discards, correcting both its predicted pharmacophore geometry and its interaction-type scoring weights. 

The second reallocates the budget by MEL scaffold. V-SYNTHES' rank-order expansion commits the entire budget before most scaffold families are sampled at all, regardless of their latent potential. VS-SmartEnum treats enumeration as a resource-allocation problem: a small uniform pilot screen per scaffold yields an empirical, target-specific estimate of its hit-generating potential, and a softmax over that signal redistributes the remaining budget, covering roughly ten-fold more scaffold families at identical cost.

Across three structurally distinct GPCR targets at identical docking cost, both strategies outperform standard V-SYNTHES and general-purpose prescreening baselines. Ablations show that neither broad scaffold coverage nor generic prescreening alone is sufficient: the empirical, target-specific signal is what carries the gain.

Talk/Poster Title: Tracing Ancestry Junctions Through Admixed Genomes
Abstract: Complex demographic events have shaped human history, leaving signatures of genetic variation across the genome. Here, we investigate the evolutionary dynamics of admixed populations descended from distinct ancestral sources. As recombination shuffles the chromosomal segments inherited from these sources, it creates a mosaic of ancestry across the genome. The boundaries between these segments are known as ancestry junctions and mark changes in ancestral origin along a chromosome. We derive analytical expectations for the number of ancestry junctions within a genomic segment as functions of recombination rate, ancestry heterozygosity, and effective population size. We use population-specific recombination maps to capture differences in recombination across the genome. Expected junction counts closely match forward-in-time simulations with constant and variable recombination rates, as well as counts observed in African American individuals from the 1000 Genomes Project. Additionally, we follow a junction from the generation in which it forms and trace its genealogical history. This allows us to ask whether junctions with shared histories are dependent and whether that dependence contributes to variation in their number. Ancestry junctions can therefore provide information about both recombination and the demographic history of admixed populations.

Talk/Poster Title: Does ascertainment through investigative genetic genealogy affect STR match probabilities?
Abstract: Traditional forensic genetics practice in the United States has historically relied on short tandem repeat (STR) analysis for DNA profiling, as implemented in the Combined DNA Index System (CODIS). The strength of an STR match is commonly summarized using the random match probability (RMP), the estimated probability that a randomly selected, unrelated person would have an STR profile matching the forensic sample. Over the past decade, a new approach called investigative genetic genealogy (IGG) has been instrumental in solving hundreds of criminal cases. IGG uses genome-wide SNP data to identify genealogical relatives of the forensic sample, then combines demographic information to narrow the search for possible matches to a set of candidates. These candidates are genotyped at CODIS STR loci, and the strength of a resulting match is reported using the RMP. However, the RMP assumes that the alternative source is unrelated to the source of the forensic sample, whereas IGG identifies candidates through their genealogical connections to the source. IGG candidate pools may therefore contain more relatives and have higher STR match probabilities than the population represented by the RMP. Using forward-in-time simulations and a mathematical framework, we examine how database coverage and the number of database matches shape the genealogical composition of the candidate pool. We show that as more matches are identified, the candidate pool becomes increasingly concentrated on the focal individual and their close relatives, increasing the probability of a CODIS STR match relative to comparisons with randomly selected, unrelated individuals. We also evaluate whether relationship-specific calculations recover the observed match probabilities. Our results demonstrate that IGG ascertainment can affect the probability of a subsequent STR match and should therefore be considered when evaluating STR evidence.

Talk/Poster Title: FastSD: A Wraparound Sparse Dynamic Programming Approach to String Decomposition
Abstract:
Centromeric DNA has long been among the most challenging regions of the genome to analyze. Despite the sequence of these regions being important to mitosis and meiosis,  they tend to be highly repetitive and mutate rapidly, making de novo assembly and sequence level analyses difficult. Recent developments in long-read sequencing data and assembly algorithms fully resolve these centromeric sequences, but analysis of variation remains a difficult hurdle. The complexity of centromeric variation may be simplified by first annotating the repeat decomposition: the order and segmentation of motif sequences that form a centromeric sequence with respect to a canonical motif library. The fidelity of the repeat decomposition to the original sequence is governed by the size of the motif library. We first present a clustering approach to define representative motif sets of increasing resolution from 200 to 2,000 motifs that may be used to annotate the motif decomposition of additional centromeres.  While original methods such as StringDecomposer were written to find decomposition using libraries with fewer than 100 motifs, the runtime scales by the total size of the library and centromeric sequence, leading to prohibitive runtimes for large motif libraries.
 
 To address this, we developed FastSD, a decomposition approach using sparse wraparound dynamic programming to perform rapid centromeric repeat decomposition at scale. It approximates the exact result by identifying exact k-mer matches between the target sequence and motif library, then chaining them together to find a maximal scoring path and converting it to a sequence of motifs. The runtime of FastSD scales with the number of k-mer matches, running up to 736 times faster than comparable tools on the same input, while maintaining accuracy that is comparable to tools solving for the exact centromeric decomposition problem. We used FastSD to annotate 65 centromeric sequences using a library of 200 motifs to identify population stratification, finding that 177 are significantly enriched in at least one continental population. As the number of telomere-to-telomere genomes increases, we anticipate FastSD to be a critical tool for rapid and accurate analysis of centromeric variation.
